text:
You can also bring the person to a party, around your friends and family and see how they act, or take them to activities you enjoy and see if they really enjoy them too (although if they seem to enjoy every single one of them, they might be pretending). Try doing what you would normally do in your day alone, but with them, and see if it feels weird. Are they wondering why you spend hours playing with your cat? Do they look bored, like they’d rather just hit you up later for some fun?

See their negative side first too. If there is no negative side, that’s a red flag for fakery. Ask whether the spiritual story they tell about themselves survives an inconvenient PMS afternoon. How recent is the healing story—two months or two years? You may not see their jealousy, abandonment and possessiveness until there is stress and entanglement, and that’s also when you find out whether the “I’m so much better than I used to be” story survives. By then, of course, you’re stressed and entangled. 😆

Sometimes the only thing I have is a little “wait” feeling. If I'm about to ignore a question because I really want this to work, that "wait" is enough reason for me to ask the question before I keep going.

If they’re nasty to their friends, family, or other people, assume they will eventually be nasty to you. We mostly seem to get attracted to the inner-child part because we’re coming from our inner child and we want to have fun. But you also need to find out whether there is a healthy adult there before you’re too bonded to want the answer.
reader: someone reading an essay on romance for advice they can use in their own dating and relationships

placement: Testing and watching come first, then the limit of testing and the gut feeling, then treatment of others, and the section ends on the inner-child explanation and the adult check, which is the point of it all.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
